name: Vector as list and arrow
statement: A vector in R^2 is two things at once — a list of two numbers and an arrow from the origin — and the two readings stay in step because addition (componentwise, tip-to-tail) and scalar multiplication (componentwise, stretching) behave identically in each reading.
aliases: a list of two numbers, and an arrow from the origin

name: Coordinates as axis recipe
statement: Every vector (x, y) equals x·e1 + y·e2 for the axis vectors e1 = (1,0) and e2 = (0,1); a vector's coordinates are not a label attached to it but its recipe in terms of the axes — x steps east, y steps north.
aliases: Every vector is a recipe out of those two

name: Parallel directions
statement: Two vectors are parallel exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other; a nonzero 2×2 determinant says exactly that the two directions are not parallel.

name: Independence of two vectors
statement: If u and v are not parallel, then au + bv = a'u + b'v forces a = a' and b = b': rearranging gives (a−a')u = (b'−b)v, and a nonzero multiple of u cannot equal a multiple of v unless both sides are zero. Perpendicularity plays no role in this.

name: Slanted coordinate grid
statement: Two non-parallel vectors u and v form a coordinate system for the plane: every point has exactly one representation a·u + b·v, read off a slanted grid of parallelograms that becomes a square grid only when the directions are perpendicular — non-perpendicularity does not break the coordinate system, it only makes the cells slanted.
aliases: perpendicularity is a convenience, not a requirement

name: Parallel collapse to a line
statement: If v is a scalar multiple of u, the set of all combinations a·u + b·v is a single line: points on that line have infinitely many representations and points off it have none.

name: Determinant, parallelism, invertibility
statement: A 2×2 matrix has determinant zero exactly when its two columns are parallel; a nonzero determinant means the columns are not parallel and the map is invertible, so every target vector has exactly one preimage.

name: Determinant-zero collapse
statement: When a 2×2 matrix has determinant zero, it squashes the whole plane onto a line — the geometric face of rank deficiency.

name: Linear map
statement: A map L is linear when it respects the two vector operations: L(u + v) = L(u) + L(v) and L(cu) = c·L(u) — add then map gives the same answer as map then add, and scale then map gives the same as map then scale; this is the whole requirement.

name: Not bending the grid
statement: Linearity is the algebraic form of not bending the grid: a linear map sends straight lines to straight lines, keeps parallel lines parallel, keeps even spacing even, and can only rotate, stretch, shear, flatten or reflect — never fold or bend.
aliases: the maps that don't bend the grid

name: Linear maps fix the origin
statement: Every linear map fixes the origin: L(0) = L(0 + 0) = L(0) + L(0) forces L(0) = 0, so any map that moves the origin is not linear.

name: Axis determination
statement: A linear map is completely pinned down by where it sends the two standard axes: L(x, y) = x·L(e1) + y·L(e2), because the axis recipe is the unique way to build a vector and linearity lets the map distribute over that sum and pull the scalars out — every other value is forced arithmetic, not a further choice.
aliases: A linear map is completely pinned down by where it sends the axes

name: Columns are axis images
statement: The columns of a matrix are exactly the images of the standard axes under the linear map it represents — first column L(e1), second column L(e2) — and that is what the numbers are, not an interpretation added on top; so reading a matrix off is reading where the axes land, with no computation required.
aliases: The columns are where the axes land
Reading a matrix is reading where the axes land

name: Matrix-vector product as column combination
statement: Multiplying a matrix by a vector means taking the linear combination of that matrix's columns weighted by the vector's entries: A(x, y) = x·col1 + y·col2 — take x copies of the first column, y copies of the second, add them.
aliases: A x is a weighted mix of the columns

name: Row-dot rule
statement: The row-dotted-with-the-vector rule computes the same thing as the column combination, only grouped differently: the k-th entry of x·col1 + y·col2 is row k dotted with the input, so the row view is a fast way to compute while the column view is the one that carries the meaning.

name: Eigenvector and eigenvalue
statement: An eigenvector of a linear map is a direction the map does not knock off its line, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the factor by which the map stretches, shrinks or flips vectors along that direction — not a multiplication by 1.
aliases: directions the map doesn't knock off their line

name: Eigendecomposition
statement: In its own eigenvector coordinates, a linear map with a full set of eigenvectors is a pure stretch along each coordinate axis — that is its eigendecomposition.

name: Least squares as projection
statement: Least-squares fitting of Ax ≈ b is the orthogonal projection of b onto the column space of A.

name: PCA directions
statement: The principal directions found by PCA are the top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix of the data — the directions in which the data varies most.

name: Singular value decomposition
statement: Every matrix factors as a rotation, then a stretch, then another rotation — the singular value decomposition — which is the eigendecomposition idea applied to AᵀA.
aliases: every matrix is rotate · stretch · rotate

name: Rank-k truncation
statement: Rank-k truncation keeps only the k largest singular components of a matrix, and this is what dimensionality reduction beyond PCA consists in.

name: Matrix multiplication as composition
statement: The matrix product BA represents the composite map "apply A first, then B", and its j-th column is B applied to the j-th column of A — because the j-th column of A is where A sends the j-th axis vector, and the composite must then send that image onward through B. Multiplying matrices is composing the maps they represent, nothing more.
aliases: the columns record one path through the two maps

name: Shear and quarter turn do not commute
statement: For the shear A = [[1,1],[0,1]] and the quarter turn B = [[0,−1],[1,0]], shearing then rotating gives BA = [[0,−1],[1,1]] while rotating then shearing gives AB = [[1,−1],[1,0]]: the same two maps applied in the two orders produce genuinely different matrices, since e1 goes 1→0→1 in the first order and 0→1→1 in the second while e2 goes 0→1→(−1,1) versus (−1,0)→(−1,0).

name: Non-commutativity
statement: Matrix multiplication is not commutative, AB ≠ BA in general, and the reason is geometric rather than a quirk of notation: the columns of a product record a path through the two maps, and two different orders of the same maps are two different paths with different outcomes.

name: Row-dot-column entry rule
statement: The (k, j) entry of a product BA is row k of B dotted with column j of A — the familiar "rows times columns" computation is exactly the composition rule read entry by entry, not a separate definition.

name: Zero product from nonzero factors
statement: A product of matrices AB can be the zero matrix even when neither A nor B is zero, because composing transformations allows one map to flatten the plane onto a line and the next to send that line to the origin — the algebraic oddity is just rank loss under composition.
aliases: AB = 0 is possible with neither factor zero

name: Span
statement: The span of a set of vectors is the set of all linear combinations of it — everything that can be built from it — and it is always a subspace through the origin: in the plane a point, a line or the whole plane, in R^3 a point, a line, a plane or all of space. A span is made of sums, not unions: the span of two non-parallel directions is the entire plane, including points that lie on neither line.

name: Linear independence
statement: A set of vectors is linearly independent when no vector in it can be built as a combination of the others — each contributes a direction the rest cannot supply; otherwise the set is dependent and its extra vectors are pure redundancy.

name: Basis and coordinates
statement: A basis is a set that is both independent and spanning — exactly enough vectors, no waste and no gaps; with respect to any basis, slanted or perpendicular, every point has exactly one recipe as a combination of the basis vectors, so coordinates are not intrinsic to a point but a description relative to a chosen basis — which is what makes a change of basis a move one can make at all.

name: Dependence test
statement: A set of vectors is dependent exactly when some non-trivial linear combination of it equals the zero vector; this algebraic test replaces eyeballing and reveals precisely which vectors are redundant.

name: Kernel as a subspace
statement: The kernel (null space) of a linear map A is the set of inputs it sends to zero, and it is always a subspace through the origin: if Ax = 0 and Ay = 0 then A(x + y) = 0, so kernels are closed under linear combination rather than being a random scatter of vectors.

name: Column space and rank
statement: For an m×n matrix, the reachable outputs are exactly the span of its columns — the column space — and the rank equals the number of independent columns, the dimension of the column space, i.e. how many dimensions of output the map actually reaches; Ax = b is solvable exactly when b lies in the column space, and nothing else governs solvability.

name: Rank–nullity
statement: Rank–nullity: rank + dim(ker A) = n for an m×n matrix — the dimensions of output reached plus the dimensions destroyed equal the dimension of the input, a conservation law.

name: Invertibility criterion
statement: For an n×n matrix A: A is invertible iff rank = n iff ker A = {0} iff det A ≠ 0 — an inverse exists exactly when nothing is lost, which is what computing a determinant is really testing.

name: Solution set as particular plus kernel
statement: If x is one solution of Ax = b, the full solution set is x plus the entire kernel: two solutions differ by a kernel vector, so the solutions are one particular solution plus a line (or plane) of sliding freedom.

name: Rank is not the column count
statement: The number of vectors says nothing about how much they span; only the number of independent directions matters, so rank answers 'how many solutions', never 'how many columns'. With three or more vectors dependence is usually a sum with assorted coefficients, invisible to the eye, and elimination detects it: the number of pivots in row echelon form is the rank, and a row of zeros is the signature of dependence.

name: Dot product as alignment
statement: u·v = Σ u_i v_i = ‖u‖‖v‖ cos θ: the sum-of-products is forced, not conventional, by applying the law of cosines to the triangle with sides u, v and u − v — the geometric and coordinate expansions of ‖u − v‖² agree on the squared lengths ‖u‖² and ‖v‖², so the leftover terms must agree, giving x₁y₁ + x₂y₂ = ‖u‖‖v‖ cos θ.

name: Consequences of the dot product identity
statement: From u·v = ‖u‖‖v‖cos θ: u·v = 0 exactly when the vectors are perpendicular or one is zero, so orthogonality is expressed as an equation; length comes free as ‖u‖ = √(u·u); and the sign reports whether the vectors lean the same way (positive) or opposed (negative), the magnitude reporting how strongly. In high-dimensional spaces such as 768-dimensional embeddings there is no picture of the angle, so cos θ = u·v/(‖u‖‖v‖) is the only definition of angle available, which is why cosine similarity is the standard similarity measure there and raw dot products must be normalized before comparison.

name: Projection formula
statement: The projection of v onto the direction u is proj_u v = (u·v / u·u) u: the coefficient c is forced by requiring the remainder v − c·u to be perpendicular to u, i.e. (v − c·u)·u = 0. The numerator measures how much of v lies along u and the denominator measures how long u is, since a long u must be stepped in smaller fractions to cover the same ground; when u is a unit vector the coefficient collapses to u·v.

name: Projection as closest point
statement: The projection c·u is the closest point on the line spanned by u: since v − c·u is perpendicular to u, Pythagoras gives ‖v − w‖² = ‖v − c·u‖² + ‖c·u − w‖² for any point w on the line, which is smallest exactly at w = c·u — the seed of least squares.

name: Projection matrix
statement: Projection onto the direction u is itself a linear map with matrix P = u·uᵀ / (uᵀu); reading its columns shows it sends u to itself and everything perpendicular to u to zero, so it keeps one line and destroys another — its rank is 1 and it is not invertible.

name: Eigenvector equation
statement: An eigenvector v of A with eigenvalue λ satisfies A·v = λ·v with v ≠ 0, equivalently (A − λI)·v = 0: eigenvectors are exactly the nonzero vectors in the kernel of A − λI, so finding them means finding the directions that A − λI collapses.

name: Composition order
statement: Three maps applied in the order A, then B, then C compose to the matrix product CBA — the rightmost factor acts first, because that is the one the input's coordinates travel through first.

name: Eigenvalues are singularity values
statement: Eigenvalues are exactly the values of λ for which A − λI is singular: the eigenvector equation (A − λI)v = 0 with v ≠ 0 says a nonzero vector is being destroyed, i.e. A − λI has a nontrivial kernel, and an invertible matrix kills only 0 and so could never be A − λI.
aliases: eigenvalues are the values of λ that make A − λI singular

name: Characteristic equation
statement: The characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0: computing the determinant with λ left symbolic gives the characteristic polynomial, whose roots are the eigenvalues, turning the abstract property 'not invertible' into a solvable equation in one unknown; once λ is fixed, its eigenvectors are the kernel of the now-singular matrix A − λI.

name: Trace and determinant checks
statement: For a 2×2 matrix the characteristic polynomial is λ² − tr(A)λ + det(A), so its eigenvalues sum to the trace and multiply to the determinant — two free arithmetic checks on any eigenvalue computation.

name: Complex and repeated eigenvalues
statement: A real matrix can have complex eigenvalues — a 90° rotation has only ±i and no real ones — and eigenvalues can repeat, so two distinct real roots cannot be expected in general.

name: Determinant as area scaling factor
statement: det A is the factor by which the linear map A scales area (volume, in higher dimensions); a map that collapses even one direction collapses all area with it, so det A = 0 exactly when a direction of input is lost. This is why the conditions 'kernel bigger than {0}', 'rank < n', 'columns dependent', 'det = 0', 'A is singular' and 'A⁻¹ does not exist' are one and the same condition, and why a solvable Ax = b then has infinitely many solutions (one particular solution plus the kernel).
aliases: det A is the factor by which A scales area

name: Diagonalization
statement: Putting the eigenvectors of A as the columns of a matrix P (so P is the map from eigen-coordinates to ordinary coordinates) and the eigenvalues on the diagonal of D gives AP = PD, hence A = PDP⁻¹: applying A is converting to eigen-coordinates with P⁻¹, stretching each axis by its λ with D, and converting back with P. All the complexity of A is carried by the two coordinate changes.

name: Powers via diagonalization
statement: The coordinate changes cancel in the middle of a product, so A^n = P D^n P⁻¹ with D^n the diagonal matrix of the λ_i^n; repeated application in the eigenbasis is nothing but independent scaling of each eigen-coefficient. Hence |λ| > 1 compounds growth, |λ| < 1 compounds decay, and a negative λ flips the sign of its component every step while its magnitude scales by |λ|^n.

name: Dominant eigenvalue
statement: Because the eigen-components evolve by the ratio (λ_i/λ_j)^n, the eigenvalue of largest modulus dominates as n grows, so A^n x points along the dominant eigenvector regardless of where it started, and the dominant eigen-direction is the direction the matrix amplifies most.

name: Dominance is out-competition
statement: The dominant eigenvector wins only because the other components present are out-grown — it does not pull anything from nothing: a starting vector with zero component along an eigenvector never acquires one, so A^n x stays in the span of the eigenvectors it actually contains.

name: Power iteration
statement: Power iteration finds the top eigenvector of a matrix too large to factor by picking a random starting vector and multiplying by A a few hundred times, then reading off the direction; it converges because the dominant eigenvalue out-competes the rest. This is how PageRank was computed and how PCA is done on data too large to form the covariance matrix explicitly.

name: Variance as a quadratic form
statement: For data centered by subtracting the mean vector, the variance along a unit direction u is the average squared projection length (1/n)Σ (x_i·u)², which equals uᵀSu with S = (1/n)XᵀX the covariance matrix — its diagonal entries are the per-feature variances and its off-diagonal entries the covariances. The whole cloud, as far as spread goes, is summarized by this one features × features symmetric matrix, however many samples there are.

name: Quadratic form is a dot product
statement: uᵀSu = u·(Su): the row-vector-times-matrix-times-column-vector sandwich is just computing Su and dotting the result with u, so the transposes are bookkeeping that lets a dot product be written in matrix form and carry no extra content.

name: Symmetric maps have orthogonal eigenvectors
statement: A real symmetric matrix S has orthogonal eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues: from Sp = λp and Sq = μq with Sᵀ = S, λ(p·q) = (Sp)·q = pᵀSᵀq = pᵀ(Sq) = μ(p·q), so (λ − μ)(p·q) = 0 and distinct eigenvalues force p·q = 0 — the grain lines of a symmetric map are perpendicular.

name: Spectral theorem
statement: Every real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and a full orthonormal eigenbasis — it can always be diagonalized by an orthogonal change of coordinates, with no defective or complex case to worry about.

name: Variance is a weighted average of eigenvalues
statement: Writing a unit direction in the orthonormal eigenbasis of the covariance matrix, u = Σ w_j p_j with Σ w_j² = 1, the quadratic form collapses to Var(u) = λ₁w₁² + λ₂w₂² + … + λ_nw_n²: a weighted average of the eigenvalues with non-negative weights summing to one. It therefore never exceeds the largest eigenvalue and attains it exactly at u = p₁, the top eigenvector.

name: PCA as optimal projection
statement: PCA chooses as its principal directions the orthonormal eigenvectors of the covariance matrix: PC1 maximizes variance and its eigenvalue is the variance captured, PC2 is the perpendicular direction capturing the most remaining variance, and so on; keeping the top k and projecting onto them is the best possible k-dimensional summary of the cloud, with variance retained (λ₁+…+λ_k)/(λ₁+…+λ_n) since the total variance is the trace.

name: Orthonormal change of basis is projection
statement: When P has orthonormal columns, PᵀP = I, so P⁻¹ = Pᵀ and the eigendecomposition reads S = PDPᵀ; the rows of Pᵀ are the eigenvectors, so the j-th coordinate of x in that basis is simply p_j·x — a change of basis to an orthonormal basis is nothing but a collection of projections.

name: Subspace
statement: A subspace is a flat set through the origin that is closed under addition and scaling; lines and planes through the origin are the basic examples (as is the origin alone), and dimension counts its independent directions — 0 for the origin alone, 1 for a line, 2 for a plane.
aliases: flat set through the origin, closed under addition and scaling

name: Line is a set, not a vector
statement: A line through the origin is not a vector but a set of vectors — all multiples {t·u : t real} of one direction u — and a plane through the origin is the set of all combinations of two independent directions, i.e. the span of two vectors; the vector supplies the direction, the line or plane is everything along it.

name: Rank as dimension of the column space
statement: The column space of a matrix is a subspace — the set of every output the map can produce — and its dimension is the rank: rank 1 means the outputs fill only a line, rank 2 a plane, and rank m the entire output space of an m-row matrix.
aliases: rank 1 means the outputs fill only a line

name: Distance as norm of a difference
statement: The ordinary distance between two vectors is the norm of their difference, ‖v − w‖, so the closest point of a set to v is the member of that set minimizing ‖v − candidate‖.
aliases: nearest in the ordinary distance sense

name: Orthogonal group O(k)
statement: For a linear map Q acting on R^k, ‖Qa−Qb‖² = ‖Qd‖² = dᵀQᵀQd with d = a−b, so all pairwise distances (hence all inner products and angles) are preserved exactly when dᵀQᵀQd = dᵀd for every d; since QᵀQ−I is symmetric, this forces QᵀQ = I. The maps preserving every inner product are therefore precisely the orthogonal group O(k) = {Q : QᵀQ = I} — all rotations, reflections and their compositions in any dimension — and no condition on det Q enters.
aliases: the family of maps that preserve all lengths and angles

name: Determinant measures volume, not geometry
statement: The determinant measures the volume scaling of a linear map, not its shape distortion: a shear with s = 0.8 has det S = 1 and preserves area, yet changes pairwise distances by roughly 43% and moves Gram-matrix entries correspondingly, and a rotation-then-shear composition is likewise det = 1 while non-orthogonal. Hence det Q = 1 does not make Q an isometry, and determinant is the wrong criterion for membership in O(k).
aliases: det = 1 is not what preserves geometry

name: Test: ‖QᵀQ − I‖_F
statement: The readout that decides whether a matrix Q lies in O(k) is ‖QᵀQ − I‖_F, which is zero for rotations and reflections and nonzero for shears and other det = 1 distortions; det Q is not this test.

name: Gram matrix K = FFᵀ
statement: For a feature matrix F ∈ R^{n×k} with one row f_i per sample, the Gram matrix is K = FFᵀ ∈ R^{n×n} with K_ij = ⟨f_i, f_j⟩: its diagonal holds squared norms ‖f_i‖² and its off-diagonals hold pairwise similarities. K is indexed by samples, not features, so it is n×n regardless of the feature dimension k — a 1024-dimensional image encoder and a 768-dimensional text encoder evaluated on the same n samples yield directly comparable matrices, differing dimensionality merely meaning some directions carry no variance.

name: K is invariant exactly under O(k)
statement: Under a change of frame F ↦ FQ the Gram matrix becomes FQQᵀFᵀ, which equals K exactly when QᵀQ = I; thus the Gram matrix is unchanged by, and only by, orthogonal transformations of the embedding.

name: Equal Gram matrices ⟺ embeddings differ by an orthogonal map
statement: If two feature matrices F and G have equal Gram matrices, then writing both via their SVDs as F = UΣVᵀ and G = UΣWᵀ pins the same U and Σ down from the common Gram matrix alone (since FFᵀ = UΣ²Uᵀ), so G = F(VWᵀ) with Q = VWᵀ orthogonal. Equal Gram matrices therefore mean the embeddings differ by an orthogonal map and nothing else, which makes 'sameness up to O(k)' the correct and only available definition of two models having 'the same representation'.

name: K is the representation with the frame factored out
statement: Because equal Gram matrices are equivalent to orthogonal equivalence, the Gram matrix is the complete record of every similarity-based judgement — nearest neighbours, retrieval, CKA, a linear probe on inner products — so two representations with the same K are indistinguishable by any such judgement. K is not a diagnostic applied to a representation; it is the representation itself with the arbitrary choice of coordinates factored out.

name: Positive-pair distribution π
statement: In a self-supervised objective whose only input is positive pairs (z, z′) ~ π, the joint distribution π — which inputs count as a match — is what determines the representation learned: not the data, but the pairing.

name: Pull-together-only losses collapse
statement: For the loss L(f) = E_{(z,z′)~π}[‖f(z) − f(z′)‖²], every term is nonnegative and the constant map f ≡ c drives all of them to zero simultaneously, so the infimum 0 is attained by a flat family of useless maps. Such a loss cannot distinguish 'the views of this image are close' from 'everything is close to everything', so any learner whose only term is a pull-together term optimizes itself into collapse.

name: Anti-collapse term manufactures the symmetry group
statement: A second, anti-collapse term is mandatory and its form fixes the residual symmetry of the representation: under the whitened-covariance constraint C_f = E[(f(z) − f̄)(f(z) − f̄)ᵀ] = I, a change of frame gives C_{Qf} = QC_fQᵀ = QQᵀ, so the constraint survives only if QQᵀ = I. The constraint thus harvests the orthogonal group O(k) out of all invertible maps — not det Q = 1, not mere invertibility — so the symmetry group of the theory is manufactured by the anti-collapse term rather than assumed. (Contrastive negatives, EMA teachers with stop-gradients, and explicit variance–covariance regularizers are alternative devices for the same job; without gradient clipping, 3 of 36 runs still collapse.)

name: The functional L_π + Ω
statement: A representation learner has the general form f* = argmin_{f∈F} E_{(z,z′)~π}[ℓ(f(z), f(z′))] + Ω(f), where π is the positive-pair distribution and the only way the data enters, ℓ is the pointwise loss on a pair (squared distance for a JEPA, an InfoNCE softmax for a contrastive learner), Ω is the anti-collapse constraint that fixes scale and shape and thereby fixes which symmetry survives, and F is the hypothesis class; SGD, batch size, learning rate and initialization appear nowhere in this expression — they are search, not objective.

name: Same functional ⇒ same minimizer set
statement: L_π + Ω is a fixed function of f that mentions no architecture, modality, image, text, ViT, ResNet or parameter count, so two learners that minimize the same functional have the same minimizer set — the same solutions up to whatever symmetry Ω failed to break; when Ω is whitening that symmetry is O(k), so their solutions agree up to a rotation.

name: Alignment criterion
statement: Two representation learners align exactly when they minimize the same functional — the same loss ℓ, the same constraint Ω, and the same positive-pair distribution π; nothing else in the recipe enters.

name: Capacity and reachability
statement: Architecture and optimization enter the analysis of a fixed objective through exactly two clauses: the hypothesis class F decides whether a minimizer exists inside the class at all (capacity), and the search procedure decides whether it is reached — these are not extra assumptions but the residue left when one asks how a fixed objective actually gets solved.

name: Cross-modal π
statement: An image encoder and a text encoder consume different inputs, so their positive-pair distributions π are distributions over different spaces; whether such cross-modal distributions still count as 'the same π' — and hence whether their representations must align up to O(k) — is itself the open question of cross-modal representational alignment rather than something settled by the objective formalism.

name: Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI)
statement: For discrete events x and y with joint probability P(x,y) and marginals P(x), P(y), the pointwise mutual information is PMI(x,y) = log[P(x,y)/(P(x)P(y))], a signed, per-pair quantity that is positive when x and y cooccur more than chance, zero when independent, and negative when depleted.

name: Mutual Information (MI) vs PMI
statement: Mutual information I(X;Y) = E_(x,y)~P[PMI(x,y)] is a nonnegative aggregate over the distribution, while PMI(x,y) is a signed, per-pair score; thus PMI carries sign information that MI cannot, making PMI the appropriate per-sample kernel target.

name: PMI as optimal contrastive score
statement: A contrastive learner deciding whether a pair (x,y) is drawn from the joint π versus independent marginals is optimally solved by the log-likelihood ratio, which equals PMI(x,y) plus a per-sample constant; thus a kernel matching PMI is forced by the discrimination task.

name: Contrastive learning estimates PMI without normalizers
statement: Contrastive objectives (e.g., NCE) estimate the ratio P(x,y)/[P(x)P(y)] by sampling negatives from the marginal, avoiding explicit computation of P(x) or its normalizer and thereby enabling practical estimation of PMI.

name: Injective renderings preserve PMI
statement: If modalities X and Y are injective functions of a shared discrete state Z (i.e., x = g_X(z), y = g_Y(z)), then PMI(x,y) = PMI(z,z′) and the optimal kernel on X equals the optimal kernel on Y, so both embeddings estimate the same PMI up to a per-sample constant.

name: Lossy renderings coarsen and weaken PMI
statement: Real observations are lossy (many-to-one) renderings of the world, merging distinct states into single observations; this coarsening strictly weakens the PMI available at the observation level by averaging associations within merged buckets.

name: Mutual k-NN alignment metric
statement: Given paired embeddings φ_i = f(x_i), ψ_i = g(y_i), the mutual k-NN score mNN(φ_i,ψ_i) = (1/k)|S(φ_i) ∩ S(ψ_i)| measures the fraction of k-nearest neighbors agreed upon by both spaces; it is used to quantify alignment and is robust across metric variants.

name: CKNNA: CKA restricted to mutual k-NN pairs
statement: CKNNA restricts CKA to pairs that are mutual k-NN in both kernels, recovering CKA as k → dim(K) and mNN when equal distances are relaxed; across 23 metric variants it shows high correlation with CKA and SVCCA, with alignment sharpening at smaller k.

name: Platonic Representation Theorem (PRT)
statement: For a shared positive-pair distribution π over world states and a whitened-covariance constraint C_f = I, the minimizer f* of the JEPA objective decomposes as f_m* ∘ g_m = Q_m h*, where h* is the common Platonic representation, Q_m is an orthogonal map per modality, and uniqueness of h* (up to rotation) requires a spectral gap in the graph Laplacian of π.

name: Graph Laplacian of positive-pair distribution
statement: Given a positive-pair distribution π over world states Z, the graph Laplacian L is defined via the weighted adjacency matrix W with entries W_ij = p(i)p(j)π(z_j|z_i), and the JEPA minimization objective corresponds to minimizing a quadratic form involving L.

name: Spectral embedding minimizes JEPA loss under gap
statement: Under the whitened-covariance constraint and with ℓ = ‖·‖², the minimizer of the JEPA objective is the k-dimensional spectral embedding Φ_π(z) = (v_1(z),…,v_k(z))/√p(z), where v_i are the eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian L corresponding to its k smallest eigenvalues; uniqueness (up to rotation) holds if and only if there is a spectral gap μ_k > μ_{k+1}.

name: Alignment bound via spectral gap and kernel mismatch
statement: If two positive-pair distributions π_1 and π_2 induce graph Laplacians with eigengaps δ_1 = μ_{k+1}(L_1) − μ_k(L_1) and δ_2 = μ_{k+1}(L_2) − μ_k(L_2), then the misalignment between their minimizers is bounded by (2√2/ min(δ_1, δ_2)) times the kernel mismatch between π_1 and π_2.

name: Kernel mismatch bounds representational drift
statement: The difference between representations learned from π_1 and π_2 is bounded by how much the PMI kernel induced by π_1 differs from that induced by π_2, scaled by the inverse of the spectral gap; thus, the data’s positive-pair distribution sets the ‘world kernel’ that constrains representational alignment.

name: Eigenvector / eigenvalue
statement: An eigenvector of a linear map (matrix) C is a nonzero vector u with Cu = λu for some scalar λ: the single test is whether the output is a scalar multiple of the input — the direction is preserved, only stretched. The zero vector is excluded (it is trivially a scalar multiple of every vector, but its direction is destroyed, not preserved), though λ = 0 is a legitimate eigenvalue.
aliases: is the output a scalar multiple of the input?

name: Surviving directions
statement: A shear bends the grid into rhombuses and turns most directions, yet preserves the lines along its own axis; even complicated high-dimensional matrices generally leave a few directions straight, and those surviving lines — not the bending chaos — are what spectral methods extract.
aliases: bending machines still have surviving directions

name: Quadratic form as weighted average of eigenvalues
statement: For a symmetric matrix C with orthonormal eigenvectors u_1,…,u_n and eigenvalues λ_1 ≥ … ≥ λ_n, a unit vector written in the eigenbasis as w = Σ_i c_i u_i has Σ_i c_i² = 1 and satisfies wᵀCw = Σ_i λ_i c_i²; the quadratic form is thus a weighted average of the eigenvalues with nonnegative weights c_i² summing to one.
aliases: variance is a weighted average of eigenvalues

name: Eigenvectors as optimizers of the quadratic form
statement: Since the weights c_i² are nonnegative and sum to one, wᵀCw ≤ λ_1 with equality only at w = ±u_1, and wᵀCw ≥ λ_n with equality only at w = ±u_n; the extreme eigenvectors are literally the maximizer and minimizer of the stretch-measuring quadratic form over unit vectors, not an algebraic accident.

name: Edge-smoothness sum as a quadratic form
statement: The edge-smoothness sum S(x) = Σ_{(i,j)∈E} (x_i − x_j)² expands, by (x_i−x_j)² = x_i² − 2x_ix_j + x_j² and regrouping, to Σ_i d_i x_i² − 2Σ_{(i,j)} x_i x_j, where d_i is the degree of vertex i — a sum over edges is secretly a quadratic form.

name: Graph Laplacian L = D − A
statement: With D the diagonal degree matrix and A the adjacency matrix, S(x) = xᵀ(D − A)x; the symmetric matrix L := D − A is the graph Laplacian.

name: Laplacian is PSD with trivial kernel vector 1
statement: The graph Laplacian is positive semidefinite — xᵀLx = Σ_{(i,j)}(x_i − x_j)² ≥ 0 is a sum of squares — and L·1 = 0 because every edge term vanishes on the constant vector; so 1 is an eigenvector of L with eigenvalue 0, and L stretches every non-constant direction precisely because the graph resists differences.

name: Zero eigenvalues count connected components
statement: xᵀLx = 0 exactly when x_i = x_j across every edge, i.e. x is constant on each connected component; hence the kernel of L is spanned by the indicator vectors of the components, and the number of zero eigenvalues of L equals the number of connected components — connectivity is read directly off the bottom of the spectrum.

name: Fiedler vector and spectral partition
statement: Among unit vectors orthogonal to 1, the minimizer of xᵀLx is the eigenvector of the smallest positive eigenvalue λ_2 (the Fiedler vector); a small λ_2 indicates an almost-disconnection, the minimizer being nearly constant on each side of the weak spot and jumping across it, so its sign pattern splits the graph into two parts.

name: Spectral embedding (Laplacian eigenmaps)
statement: Stacking the bottom non-trivial eigenvectors x_2,…,x_{k+1} of the Laplacian as coordinates — vertex i mapped to (x_2(i),…,x_{k+1}(i)) ∈ ℝ^k — gives the spectral embedding, also called Laplacian eigenmaps, in which densely connected vertices land close together and weakly connected regions drift apart.

name: Degree domination of the raw Laplacian
statement: In the raw Laplacian's quadratic form a vertex of degree d contributes d·x_i², so a single heavily connected hub dominates S(x) and can twist the minimizer all by itself, since the form measures variation counted by edges.

name: Smoothness per step of travel
statement: Smoothness of a function on a graph means its values change little per step of travel across the graph, with every vertex counting once rather than once per incident edge.

name: Normalized Laplacian
statement: The normalized Laplacian N = I − D^{−1/2}AD^{−1/2} satisfies xᵀNx = Σ_{(i,j)∈E} (x_i/√d_i − x_j/√d_j)², each edge comparing degree-scaled values so that a hub's many edges dilute its influence per edge and per-step variation is measured fairly.

name: T_π = I − N_π
statement: For a weighted adjacency matrix Π (entries counting how often vertices occur as positive pairs) with degree matrix D, the operator T_π = D^{−1/2}ΠD^{−1/2} equals I − N_π, where N_π = I − D^{−1/2}ΠD^{−1/2} is the corresponding normalized Laplacian.

name: Top of T_π is bottom of N_π
statement: Because T_π = I − N_π, the top eigenvectors of T_π (eigenvalues near 1) are exactly the bottom eigenvectors of N_π (eigenvalues near 0), so a large T_π eigenvalue corresponds to a smooth direction of the graph — the same content with the sign flipped.

name: Top-k embedding matrix F
statement: The top-k spectral embedding takes the top-k eigenvectors u_1,…,u_k of T_π, scales them by D^{1/2}, and stacks them as the columns of a matrix F having one row per vertex, so that the i-th row of F is the embedding of vertex i in ℝ^k.

name: Eigenvector freedoms: line, not arrow; eigenspace basis
statement: An eigenvector equation Cu = λu fixes only the line, not the arrow — u, −u, and cu are all solutions — and when eigenvalues tie, any orthonormal basis of the eigenspace is equally valid, so two valid embeddings of the same vertex set necessarily differ by F′ = FQ with Q orthogonal (with distinct eigenvalues only the sign flips survive).

name: Embedding determined only up to orthogonal transformation
statement: Since F′(F′)ᵀ = FQQᵀFᵀ = FFᵀ for orthogonal Q, the Gram matrix of the embedding is untouched; the spectral embedding is therefore determined only up to an orthogonal transformation Q, and the invariant object is the Gram matrix FFᵀ — the geometry, not the coordinates.

name: Pairwise distances are rotation-invariant
statement: Under a valid change of embedding, rows transform as f_i ↦ f_iQ, so the difference between two vertex embeddings becomes (f_i − f_j)Q, whose length is unchanged because an orthogonal map preserves lengths; hence all pairwise distances between embedded vertices survive sign flips and rotations of eigenvector columns — the cloud moves but is never stretched or shrunk.

name: Top-k set changes only at the cut-off
statement: For a spectral embedding built from the k largest eigenvectors, the only place an additive error can change which vectors belong to the embedding is the cut-off boundary between μ_k and μ_{k+1}; every other eigenvalue separation, including the spacing above the leading eigenvalue μ_1, is already settled, so an error there cannot reopen the choice of the set.
aliases: the only place an error can change which vectors are in that set is the boundary

name: Near-tie frees the boundary eigenvectors
statement: When μ_k and μ_{k+1} are nearly equal, eigenvectors k and k+1 are no longer separately determined — the freedom to choose any orthonormal basis within a tied eigenspace becomes live — so any perturbation supplies a new mixing angle between them, whereas a genuine gap makes that freedom inert by fixing the subspace.

name: Stability margin at the cut-off
statement: A perturbation of size ‖E‖ rotates the top-k eigenspace by at most on the order of ‖E‖ / (μ_k − μ_{k+1}): the gap at the cut-off sits in the denominator and is the stability margin of the embedding, so a small gap turns any error into an arbitrary rotation and a large gap pins the embedding down up to a small, recoverable rotation.
aliases: the gap at the cut-off is the stability margin of the embedding

name: μ_1 does not govern embedding stability
statement: The magnitude of the leading eigenvalue does not determine the stability of a spectral embedding: two operators can share μ_1 = 0.99 exactly yet have boundary gaps of 0.80 and 0.01, giving an error ε = 0.01 a rotation of about 1% in the first case (stable) and about 100% in the second (destroyed), so any stability criterion keyed to μ_1 is invalid.
aliases: Identical μ_1 = 0.99 in both, wildly different outcomes

name: Finite sample, whole domain
statement: A dataset is a finite list of input–output pairs, while what is asked of a learner is a function over the whole (typically continuous) domain; with n samples there are always unsampled points — at n = 10⁹ as surely as at n = 10 — so the gap between what is given and what is asked never closes.

name: Generalization as an added claim
statement: The data determine function values only at the sampled inputs; at any unsampled point every value is consistent with them, so generalization is never a matter of reading off but always of adding a claim about how unseen points relate to seen ones — and every learning method is a different such claim.

name: Curse of dimensionality reframed
statement: The curse of dimensionality is not that data are scarce but that in high dimension the claims a learner is forced to add become either implausible or unaffordable.

name: Smoothness gives no size
statement: Smoothness does not bound the value at an unsampled point: with samples (−1, 0) and (1, 0), every function f_A(x) = A(1 − x²) matches the data for any real A, and all of them are infinitely differentiable, so f(0) is unconstrained. Continuity and differentiability assert the existence of derivatives, not their size, and a bound on f(x₀) needs a size.

name: Lipschitz bound
statement: A Lipschitz condition |f(x) − f(x′)| ≤ L|x − x′| is what licenses an error bound, since interpolating from the nearest sample input xᵢ gives |f(x₀) − f(xᵢ)| ≤ L·d(x₀, xᵢ) — a bound proportional to the distance to the nearest sample; without a finite number L the bound reads L = ∞ and is vacuous.

name: Rate versus covering
statement: A rate and a coverage condition do different jobs: a rate L converts distance into error — given a sample input within δ, the error there is at most Lδ — but it says nothing about whether sample inputs within δ of every point can be afforded; the exponential cost lives in the covering, not in the rate.

name: No empirical ceiling on the rate
statement: A rate L cannot be established from data: every finite sample is compatible with a function whose true rate exceeds anything observed, with the excess hidden between sample inputs, so the data give a floor under L but never a ceiling — noise-free observation and regular spacing change nothing.

name: Metric, rate, coverage
statement: A guarantee about an unseen point requires exactly three things: a metric d, a rate L in that metric, and coverage in that metric; the same metric must serve both the rate and the coverage or Lδ does not compute, and nothing about the data supplies any of the three.

name: Methods as metric–rate–coverage instances
statement: Seemingly unrelated methods are the same guarantee with different assumptions substituted: Lipschitz regression assumes a rate L in Euclidean distance on ℝ^D; a linear model assumes the far stronger exact linearity with L = ‖w‖; k-NN assumes a label rate in whatever feature metric was chosen; manifold learning assumes a rate per unit of intrinsic distance along the manifold.

name: Ambient versus intrinsic distance
statement: Ambient distance is the straight-line distance ‖x − x′‖ in the ℝ^D the data sit in, while intrinsic distance is measured along the manifold — arc length on the surface; the two rulers disagree wherever the manifold curves.

name: Metric choice selects the hypothesis class
statement: The metric is the lever: it decides which pairs count as nearby and therefore which functions are admitted, so an intrinsically smooth function is under no obligation to vary slowly per unit of ambient distance — choosing between the rulers is choosing how fast f may move between points the ambient ruler calls close.

name: The curse lives in the metric
statement: Because the metric is something one chooses, the curse of dimensionality is a statement about d rather than a statement about the data, and d is up for selection.

name: Intrinsic dimension is not rank
statement: Intrinsic dimension k does not imply that the data span a k-dimensional linear subspace: a k-dimensional manifold is only locally a k-plane, curvature pushes variance into the normal directions, and 'covariance rank = k' is a global linear-subspace claim that manifold structure does not support.

name: Short circuits
statement: Where a manifold folds, the ambient distance between points on different sheets can be smaller than the intrinsic distance along the surface, so an ambient-metric neighbourhood selects the wrong points — the cross-sheet neighbours instead of the along-surface ones.

name: Distance concentration
statement: The small-n picture of inter-point distances — maximum ≈ √d from the cube diagonal, minimum ≈ 0 — is not the high-dimensional behaviour: at fixed n both extremes concentrate, so distance contrast does not explode and nearness carries little information.

name: Two failure modes
statement: The curse of dimensionality is two failures that fail differently: a counting failure, where the number of samples needed to put one near every point is unaffordable, and a geometry failure, where samples are affordable but 'near' has stopped meaning anything — each admitting a different kind of remedy.

name: Price of the manifold hypothesis
statement: The formal price of the manifold hypothesis is three conditions: smoothness, bounded curvature, and no short circuits.

name: Intrinsic sample-complexity rate
statement: Minimax rates for manifold estimation scale as (1/n)^{2/(2+d)}, with the intrinsic dimension d in the exponent and the ambient dimension D absent from it, so the sample complexity is governed by intrinsic rather than ambient dimension.

name: Intrinsic dimension of real data
statement: ImageNet measures at intrinsic dimension 26–43 against 150,528 pixel dimensions, and at d = 40 the rate exponent is 2/42 ≈ 0.048 — low by roughly a factor of five thousand, and still hopeless for bounds exponential in d.

name: Empirical limits of the manifold hypothesis
statement: The manifold hypothesis is literally false as stated and survives only as an idealization refined five ways: real data are a stratified union of manifolds of differing dimension (MNIST 2s and 8s need different numbers of factors), data lie near rather than on the manifold, intrinsic dimension is defined only at a scale (noise inflates fine-scale estimates while coarse scales stabilize), the estimators themselves are contested and sensitive to k, noise, curvature and sample size, and a manifold structure is rejected outright for the token embeddings of several large language models.

name: Productive but incomplete idealization
statement: The correct standing of the manifold hypothesis is that it is a productive but incomplete idealization whose loose ends are live problems — not a true premise from which low-dimensional learning follows.

name: Euclidean default as recording choice
statement: Euclidean distance ‖x − x′‖ is the ruler coordinates come with by default, but it is a recording choice rather than a property of the data: units (millimetres versus metres, raw pixel values versus calibrated radiance), feature scaling (normalizing a feature stretches its axis), and encoding (one-hot versus ordinal codes for the same category) all leave the information the same while changing the geometry, and the neighbour structure moves with it.
aliases: it is a recording choice, not a property of the data

name: Axis stretch flips neighbours
statement: Stretching a single coordinate axis by a factor such as 10× can flip completely which points are nearest to a query — from the points beside it to the points above and below it — although nothing about the data has changed, only the ruler.
aliases: stretch a single coordinate axis by 10× and the points nearest to a query can flip completely

name: Nearest neighbour is not a data property
statement: 'Nearest neighbour' is not a property of a dataset but of the dataset together with its units, so every method that reasons from neighbours — which is nearly all of them — is built on a choice nobody made deliberately; the same holds for the hypothesis class a metric selects, since a different ruler admits different functions.
aliases: "nearest neighbour" is not a property of your dataset. It's a property of your dataset and your units

name: Invariance asymmetry
statement: There is an asymmetry among facts about a dataset under invertible changes of coordinates: how many independent directions actually generate the variation is untouched by any such change, whereas distances are not — so dimension-like quantities survive a change of ruler while the geometry of nearness does not.
aliases: Some facts about a dataset are untouched by any invertible change of coordinates ... Distances are not among them

name: Build on invariants
statement: Because coordinate-invariant quantities such as the number of independent directions of variation survive every invertible change of coordinates while distances do not, a principled remedy for the arbitrariness of the ruler must be built on those invariants rather than on any particular chosen distance.
aliases: That asymmetry is going to be the whole fix

name: Manifold (chart definition)
statement: A set M ⊂ ℝ^D is a k-dimensional manifold if around every point p ∈ M there is a neighbourhood U and a smooth bijection φ: U → ℝ^k onto an open set with smooth inverse — a chart — so that locally k coordinates suffice and nothing global (no global coordinate system, no global product structure) is required. Whether a given set is a manifold is proved by exhibiting charts at every point or showing some point has none: a line, parabola, circle or helix is 1-dimensional, a plane, sphere or torus is 2-dimensional, ℝ^D is its own chart, while two crossing lines (xy = 0) fail at the origin, where every neighbourhood is an X rather than an interval.

name: Locally flat, globally curved
statement: The chart cover is finite and cannot always be reduced to one: the circle needs two overlapping charts (the arc missing the top and the arc missing the bottom) and no cleverness reduces that to a single chart, although every point on it has a small arc as a neighbourhood — this gap between "locally an interval everywhere" and "globally a circle" is what global curvature means, and it is not what inflates the counting exponent. At each point there is a tangent k-plane that rotates smoothly as the point moves; the manifold is the set itself, not the union of its tangent planes.

name: Covering count (1/δ)^D
statement: Covering the unit cube [0,1]^D to within δ in Euclidean distance requires on the order of (1/δ)^D sample inputs: the cube is a product of D independent intervals, so the cells needed along each axis multiply rather than add, and the exponent is the number of directions one can move in (the dimension). The argument is deterministic pigeonhole reasoning with no probability anywhere — cut space into cells of side 2δ; an empty cell's centre lies at distance at least δ from every sample outside it, so coverage forbids empty cells — and constants such as 2 or π are irrelevant to the conclusion.

name: Resolution scaling law
statement: Halving the tolerance multiplies the required sample count by 2^D: N(δ/2) = 2^D·(1/δ)^D = 2^D·N(δ), and each extra axis at fixed δ multiplies the count by another 1/δ. Finer resolution never needs fewer points, so any computation that makes the requirement shrink when the tolerance is tightened has a reciprocal flipped.

name: Assumption mandatory in every dimension
statement: The need for an assumption is dimension-independent: with no assumption on f, no sample count suffices in any dimension, so learning is equally impossible in one dimension as in a hundred. Dimension does not decide whether an assumption is required — it decides only what an assumption costs, so the curse of dimensionality is a claim about price rather than about possibility.

name: Learner blindness to the true function
statement: A learner sees only the sample, never which function is true, so it cannot help but be fooled: for whatever it returns there is a competing function that agrees on every sampled input and differs off the sample, and an adversary can choose it. This is why no amount of data and no clever algorithm closes the gap without an assumption.

name: Adaptivity exploits, does not create
statement: Adaptivity cannot substitute for an assumption — active sampling does not create structure the data do not have — but given an assumption it can beat the passive covering count.

name: Rigidity buys discount
statement: Assumptions about f trade rigidity against price, and the more an assumption claims the cheaper the guarantee it buys: assuming exact linearity in D features costs D + 1 points for an exact determination with no ε at all, a bound on the rate of change L per Euclidean unit in ℝ^D costs ~(L/ε)^D samples, and a bound on the rate per unit of distance along a k-dimensional manifold costs ~(L/ε)^k samples.

name: Curse as price, not possibility
statement: "The sample count must grow with dimension" is true but inert, since the guarantee is a theorem either way; the operative question is whether the required growth is affordable, and what varies between settings is a price attached to the assumption rather than the possibility of a guarantee.

name: Unaffordability at scale
statement: At ε = 0.1 the covering requirement is 10^5 samples at D = 5 (affordable against the 10^6 available) but 10^500 samples at D = 500 — a factor of 10^495 larger and far beyond the ~10^80 atoms in the observable universe — so no collection of data closes the gap, and "grow with dimension" is off by hundreds of orders of magnitude rather than merely loose.

name: Chord–arc comparability
statement: The inequality ‖x − x′‖ ≤ d_M(x, x′) is free, since a chord is never longer than an arc; the reverse comparability of intrinsic and ambient distance is an assumption that holds only locally and under bounded curvature.

name: Source of the ε^-k discount
statement: The ε^(−k) sample discount comes from covering the manifold in its own k dimensions, not from the ambient–intrinsic comparability bound; that bound's role is to let a method working in ambient coordinates access the discount, at the cost of a constant factor.

name: Counting on a manifold
statement: Counting coverage on a k-dimensional manifold gives N ≈ (number of charts)·(1/δ)^k: inside one chart the manifold is a product of k coordinates, so it takes the same (1/δ)^k cells as a k-cube, while the number of charts is fixed by how fast the tangent plane rotates — a property of M, not of δ — so it does not grow as δ → 0, and curvature, size and shape enter only the front constant (the circle: 2 charts give ~20 cells at δ = 0.1 and ~2000 at δ = 0.001). The exponent k, not the chart count, governs whether the requirement is survivable; with unbounded curvature the chart count blows up, so bounded curvature (a reach condition) is a real assumption rather than housekeeping.

name: Rank as linear shadow of intrinsic dimension
statement: Covariance rank is invariant only under invertible linear changes of coordinates (units, rescaling arrives in this class) whereas intrinsic dimension is invariant under any smooth invertible change, linear or not: a nonlinear change of coordinates can bend a line into a curve and raise the rank while the intrinsic dimension stays 1, so rank is a linear shadow of the structural quantity rather than the quantity itself.

name: Rescaling reweights features
statement: Stretching a feature by a factor s multiplies its squared differences by s², so agreement in that feature dominates the distance decision while separation in the other features becomes almost free; rescaling does not distort the data, it reweights which features decide nearness — whoever writes the units writes the neighbour graph.

name: Rank is affine-hull dimension
statement: The covariance rank of a point cloud equals the dimension of its affine hull — the number of independent directions the points actually span. If a set M lies in a k-plane its rank is k; if M is curved no k-plane contains it, so its rank is strictly greater than k; rank = k holds exactly in the flat case.

name: Local versus global scope
statement: Covariance rank and intrinsic dimension are quantities of different scope: covariance rank is one global number for the whole dataset, whereas intrinsic dimension k is local — one number per point — and is the same number at every point only because the set is a manifold.

name: The ε^-k discount is local
statement: The ε^(−k) sample discount is a local fact, obtained from a chart, a neighbourhood and a tangent plane, while the affine hull is a global fact; the two disagree for every curved manifold — and data are curved in the generic case — so the global covariance rank gives no access to the discount.

name: Local covariance recovers the tangent plane
statement: In a sufficiently small neighbourhood of a point p the manifold is flat, so the covariance computed on that neighbourhood has rank k and its k principal directions give the tangent plane at p, whereas the same data taken globally has rank equal to the ambient dimension and reveals no such structure.

name: PCA is not manifold learning
statement: "Run PCA and keep k components" is not manifold learning: PCA fits a single global linear subspace, so it cannot capture low-dimensional structure that lives in local subspaces differing from point to point.
